item.description:

Some experiments with using LLMs in Emacs, and a demo of gptel's presets feature. We can do better than a linear, immutable, top-down chat interface to LLMs. gptel is an LLM client for Emacs. (https://gptel.org) A preset is a named collection of gptel settings and behaviors applied to an LLM query as a unit: they can change any aspect of LLM interaction on the fly, providing a flexible, customizable interface for most (text-based) things you'd need an LLM for. 00:13 LLMs as text transformations 01:19 LLM clients as shell commands 02:03 Software with too many options 03:00 Configuration files and (finally) a gptel preset 03:10 The tutor preset 04:31 Inside the Tutor preset 05:12 The Introspect preset 06:52 The JSON preset 07:35 Interlude I: How presets work 08:52 Redirection: source | gptel | destination 10:04 Source: the Expand preset 11:20 The Visible-Text preset 11:55 The Include preset 12:48 Interlude II: Adding dynamic behavior to presets 14:14 Destination: the Notify preset 14:51 The Rewrite preset 17:05 The Annotate preset 21:18 Presets as "agents" 24:37 Problems with the presets UI 26:02 Interlude III: Resources for presets 27:22 LLM UIs in Emacs: this ain't it Emacs packages showcased in this demo: - https://github.com/karthink/gptel - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-agent - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-annotate - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-preset-collection - https://github.com/kmontag/macher Emacs packages and settings used in this demo - Presentation software: https://github.com/positron-solutions/dslide - Visuals: https://github.com/minad/org-modern and https://github.com/rnkn/olivetti - Fancy Flymake UI: https://github.com/konrad1977/flyover - Font: Monaspace Neon - Emacs theme: ef-reverie ,#emacs #llm #llms #gptel

,### Install ```emacs-lisp (use-package project :ensure nil :custom (project-vc-extra-root-markers '(".project"))) ``` ,### Project Core Commands * `C-x p f` : `project-find-file` - Search and open a file inside the current project. * `C-x p p` : `project-switch-project` - Switch to another project from your list of known projects. * `C-x p b` : `project-switch-to-buffer` - Switch to an open buffer belonging only to this project. * `C-x p d` : `project-dired` - Open a Dired directory buffer at the root of the project. * `C-x p g` : `project-find-regexp` - Search for a text string or regex across all project files. * `C-x p e` : `project-eshell` - Open a dedicated Eshell terminal instance at the project root. * `C-x p c` : `project-compile` - Run a build or compile command from the project root directory. * `C-x p k` : `project-kill-buffers` - Close all open buffers associated with the current project. ,### Project Management * `M-x project-forget-project` : Remove a specific directory from Emacs' remembered project list. * `M-x project-forget-projects-under` : Remove all saved projects under a specific directory. * `M-x project-forget-zombie-projects` : Automatically remove all non-existent or deleted project directories from the saved list. ,### Other videos on this topic * https://youtu.be/6PlrXQ0tnQM?si=ELMnp_ZpwXSQhMZa * https://www.youtube.com/live/O6hMwJfaXV8?si=lbG6gf4vVatyFQSu

item.title: Emacs: Completion in the buffer with completion-at-point-functions
item.description:
youtube

In this ~22-minute video I explain how Emacs performs completion in a buffer. I cover what happens behind the scenes with the variable completion-at-point-functions. Then I also go to the frontends, which affects the modalities of interaction. I cover the built-in Completions buffer, the packages Corfu and Company, and the built-in completion-preview-mode. Finally, I comment at some further length on how to control the grouping of results in the completion-at-point-functions. In that context I also mention the Cape package, as well as some extra functionality that the Company package provide. I wrote an article which covers all of what is in the video as well as code samples. You can read it on my website here: https://protesilaos.com/codelog/2026-07-19-emacs-completion-at-point-functions/

item.title: Full IDE Power Over SSH: Remote C++ Development with Just a Terminal and Emacs
item.description:
youtube

Everything in this video runs over a plain SSH connection to a remote Linux box — no GUI, no forwarded X11, no VS Code Remote extension. Just a terminal, SSH, and Emacs configured as a full C++ IDE. I walk through: • Symbol navigation — jump to definitions across your own code and the C++ standard library, find every reference, and jump back out, all without leaving the keyboard • Refactoring — project-wide rename backed by clangd, not text search-and-replace • Debugging — breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, stepping, live variable inspection, and expression evaluation via DAP (lldb/gdb), fully interactive over a terminal session The point isn't "Emacs is old-school" — it's that terminal + SSH + Emacs is a genuinely fast, lightweight way to work on remote code: no laggy remote-GUI protocol, no heavyweight remote-extension server, works the same whether you're on a fast connection or a rough one. Config used in this video (MIT licensed, free to use/fork): https://github.com/jclosure/vscode-flavored-emacs-2026 ,#emacs #ssh #cpp #remotedevelopment #terminal #linux #debugging #clangd #vscode #dape
